04 Checking the field numbers

“10 litres an hour” is more than a 9.9 hp engine can burn. We size from the engine, not the fuel can

What it means

The Yamaha EK9.9D is rated at 7.3 kW at 5,000 rpm. Even at a realistic 15% efficiency, 96 kW of fuel would give about 14 kW at the shaft, nearly twice its rating. The 10 L/h field figure covers more than this one engine’s use.

Design basis we use

The 9.9 hp engine works at part throttle on the travel legs: 4–5 kW at the shaft. This is confirmed by logging its own fuel flow and rpm during the survey.

Why it matters

Sizing from “10 L/h” would roughly double the battery, its cost and its weight for no benefit.

05 Hull and speed

A displacement hull: past 6 knots, each extra knot costs power steeply

≈ 6 kn
cruise speed implied by 8–10 nm in about 1.5 h
Fn 0.33
Froude number at 6 kn. The boat pushes through the water instead of skimming over it, so speed tops out near 7 kn

The model uses an admiralty-coefficient fit, with a wave-making penalty above 6.2 kn, calibrated to the reported fuel use. It gets replaced by measured speed vs. power from GPS and shaft-load logging in the first trials.

Holding cruise at 5.5–6 kn instead of 7 kn cuts the power needed by about half. The fishermen keep their schedule, and battery size drops sharply.

09 Motor equivalence

Why a 6 kW-class electric motor does the job of a 9.9 hp kerosene engine

Compare the thrust the propeller delivers, not the label power. A large, slow electric propeller wastes less power pushing a heavy displacement boat.

Same push or better

Makers publish 2.9–3.5 kW of propulsive power for 6 kW-class motors, against ≈ 2.9 kW for the EK9.9D.

More pull at low speed

≈ 41 Nm at the propeller from zero rpm, against 12–30 Nm for the EK9.9D, which stalls below idle. This matters for net hauling and beaching.

All day, not peak

Electric ratings are continuous; the EK9.9D reaches 7.3 kW only at 5,000 rpm. Cruise needs ≈ 4.5 kW: 92% of a 6 kW-class rating, 60% of an 8 kW-class.

Electric: 4.9 kW shaft (Torqeedo manual); propulsive 3.5 kW (Torqeedo), 2.9 kW (ePropulsion). EK9.9D: 7.3 kW at prop shaft (Yamaha); its propeller efficiency estimated.

10 Electric outboard

13 Propeller matching

A slow-turning, high-pitch propeller puts the operating point inside the continuous rating

Propeller absorption rises with the cube of rpm. With a 6 kW-class motor, cruise sits at about 92% of the continuous shaft rating, so pitch must be chosen carefully. An 8 kW-class motor brings it to about 60% and leaves real headroom for head seas.

Pilot carries two propellers

A high-pitch cruise prop for normal 3–5 t trips. On heavy catch days the demand curve rises (grey); a lower-pitch thrust prop brings it back under the green line. A thrust-prop option is a selection criterion.

Bollard pull check

Static thrust is measured on the slipway against the existing engine before any sea trial. It sets the net-hauling and beaching margin.

14 Battery sizing

A 24 kWh swappable set covers the trip; the second engine is the reserve

Chemistryopen: LFP or NMC (next slide)
Voltage48 V class, below 60 V DC
Current at 6 kW≈ 120 A at 48–51 V
Cycle life at 1 cycle/day1,500–8,000 · 6–12+ years
Mass vs. field limit≈ 165–200 kg / 300 kg

No separate battery reserve: the second engine already on board brings the boat home. Ageing is handled in the swap pool, where modules are retired at 80% capacity. A 6 kW-class motor at full throttle for 3 h (≈ 19 kWh) still fits; an 8 kW-class motor is limited to cruise power.

What electric boats use

Torqeedo’s Deep Blue moved from NMC to LFP. ePropulsion, Mercury Avator and Navalt (Kerala) use LFP. Kochi Water Metro chose LTO for 10-minute charging. IRS rules (2024) accept any chemistry tested to IEC 62619.

Heat matters more than chemistry: LFP cell life falls from 6,000 to 2,500 cycles at 45 °C, so the pack is shaded and ventilated.

18 Weight, placement and trim

Battery goes low and amidships, not at the transom

Net effect on weight

Battery ≈ 190 kg (LFP; NMC ≈ 170 kg) plus an electric outboard (≈ 30 kg typical, 22–55 kg across the shortlist), minus the EK9.9D (40 kg) and fuel cans ≈ 30 kg. About 150 kg extra in total.

Against payload

150 kg is about 2% of the boat's 7–10 t capacity, about the weight of two to three crew.

Why amidships

Weight at the transom squats the stern, reduces freeboard aft and drags the hull. Near the CG, trim barely changes.

Who builds it

FRP-bonded bearers and a raised, drained tray, made by the local boat builder and checked with an inclining test.

20 Electrical single-line diagram

One power path for driving, one for charging, and the BMS watches every cell

21 Fault responses

Every fault has a defined, safe response

FaultResponse
Short circuitModule fuses + main fuse clear (sized above motor peak current)
Cell over/under-voltageBMS opens K2 when charging, K1 when driving
Modules mismatched at swapBMS keeps contactors open until module voltages match
Over-currentController derates; shunt reading lets BMS open K1
Cell over-temperatureDerate at 50 °C; BMS opens K1/K2 at 60 °C
Insulation lossIsolation monitor alarm on the display
Man overboardKill-switch lanyard or stop key pulled: torque to zero, K1 opens
Low SoCWarn at 30%, limp mode at 15%
Any other faultFail safe: torque to zero, K1 open, alarm shown

Fail safe by design

Any fault ends in the same state: torque to zero and contactors open. The boat drifts safely; it never runs away.

The fisherman sees it

Every alarm shows on the tiller display and is logged with time and position for the Department’s review.

22 Built for salt, spray and beaching

The sea is the hardest test condition. We design for it first

IP67 enclosures

Battery, controller and connectors survive brief submersion. The pack sits on a raised tray above bilge water.

Corrosion

316 stainless fasteners, hard-anodised aluminium, a zinc anode on the leg, and conformal-coated boards.

Vibration and slamming

Cells clamped in compression and the enclosure on rubber mounts. Shock tests follow IEC 60068-2-27 practice.

Heat

The pack runs at only about 0.2C at full power, so cells stay cool in 35 °C ambient. Shaded, ventilated tray. No charging above 45 °C.

Gas venting

Pressure-relief vent routed overboard, away from crew and the fuel cans.

Standards reference

IEC 62619 (cells), ISO 16315 (electric propulsion), IEC 60529 (IP rating).

23 How the fisherman uses it

Same tiller, same habits. Three modes, picked by the throttle

The fisherman steers and twists the grip exactly as he does today. The controller limits power to protect the battery and the motor.

Harbour, beaching, net hauling

0–2 kW, fine control. Silent, instant reverse, holds the boat steady at the net. No petrol needed to start or idle.

Travel to and from the ground

About 4.5 kW at the shaft. About 92% of a 6 kW-class continuous rating, 60% of an 8 kW-class, for the 1.5-hour legs, the job the 9.9 hp engine does today.

Boost and get-home

Short peak boost, per the selected motor, to launch through the surf. Below 15% SoC the controller limits power; the second engine on board is the get-home backup.

24 Charging

Modules are swapped as a set and recharged overnight on an ordinary single-phase supply

Energy from grid per trip≈ 19.5 kWh
Charger3.3 kW · 230 V · 16 A
Window ashore≈ 14 h
Cost at ₹8/kWh≈ ₹155 per trip

Pilot

Modules come off as a matched set and charge in a shaded, ventilated bay at the landing centre. About 1.2 sets per boat cover spares and repairs.

Scale-up

A shared charging bay at the fish landing centre. About 4 kWp of rooftop solar per boat covers the daily energy on Tamil Nadu sun.

25 Charging in place: earthing

Swapping keeps the grid off the boat. Any boat charged in place needs its own earthing plan

No shock on a wet deck

30 mA RCD at the shore pillar. Charger with galvanic isolation between grid and battery. Type A or B RCD as the charger's DC leakage requires.

No corrosion of the leg

A galvanic isolator in the protective earth blocks the small DC currents that would eat the motor leg and anode, while still passing fault current. An isolation transformer is the fleet option if pilot readings show corrosion.

Floating battery, monitored

The 48 V pack is not connected to the hull or shore earth. The BMS checks insulation and alarms on a fault. Charging runs only when the BMS allows it, and never above 45 °C.

Refs: IEC 60364-7-709, ISO 13297, ISO 16315.

28 Pilot and validation

Two boats, two months, real fishing, with the Department watching the data

Logged every trip, automatically
  • GPS track, speed and time per leg
  • Electric kWh, peak and average kW, SoC before and after
  • Cell and motor temperatures, every alarm and fault
  • Kerosene and petrol still bought, from the fuel log
  • Charging time and energy from the grid; swap time per set
  • Load, crew and sea state on every trip

Fishermen's feedback on control, weight, charging and usability is recorded weekly. Their view is a pass criterion, not an afterthought.

  • Freeboard and trim at normal load

Existing propulsion

  • EK9.9D gear ratio, fitted propeller diameter and pitch
  • RPM at cruise on each leg
  • Fuel flow of the 9.9 hp engine on each leg
  • Steering and throttle arrangement

Operation and site

  • Crew, payload, catch on typical days
  • Sea state, current and wind on trips
  • Spray and bilge exposure zones
  • Shore power at the landing point
  • Local Department requirements
